title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: Existing R packages pvaluefunctions concurve visualize p-values two dimensions. show p-value changes one parameter time — typically effect size, given fixed standard error. p3d package extends three dimensions, showing p-value function effect size sample size simultaneously. vignette compares two approaches.

title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: compare 2D p-value curve (pvaluefunctions) 3D p-value surface (p3d), using scenario: Observed effect size: d = 0.5 Sample size: n = 30

title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: pvaluefunctions package visualizes p-value function single parameter. First, need install : Now compute 2D curve: resulting plot shows p-value function estimated effect size, observed effect size (0.5) center. curve symmetric minimum observed effect size.
code: install.packages("pvaluefunctions") library(pvaluefunctions)  conf_dist(   estimate = 0.5,   stderr = 1 / sqrt(30),   df = 29,   tstat = 0.5 * sqrt(30),   type = "ttest",   plot_type = "p_val" )

title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: p3d package visualizes p-value function effect size sample size:  3D surface reveals structure 2D curve : p-value symmetric n. n increases, surface flattens toward zero large |d| toward one near d = 0. significance boundary curve, point. n, critical effect size d_crit(n) p-value falls 0.05. Sample size moderates effect d. small n, large effects significant. large n, even small effects become significant.
code: surface <- p_surface(   d = seq(-2, 2, 0.1),   n = seq(5, 200, 5) )  plot_p_static(surface)

title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: Let’s place 2D curve 3D surface side side. 2D curve corresponds slice 3D surface n = 30:  2D curve mathematically equivalent slice 3D surface n = 30. give p-value d = 0.5:
code: # 2D curve at n = 30 curve_30 <- p_curve_2d(d = seq(-2, 2, 0.1), n = 30)  # Plot the 2D curve plot(curve_30$d, curve_30$p, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "darkred",      xlab = "Effect size (d)", ylab = "p-value",      main = "2D p-value curve (n = 30)") abline(h = 0.05, col = "blue", lty = 2) grid() curve_30$p[curve_30$d == 0.5] #> [1] 0.01043739 surface$p[surface$d == 0.5, surface$n == 30] #> [1] 0.01043739

title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: 2D curve hides moderating effect sample size. Consider effect size (d = 0.5) three different sample sizes: n = 10, p-value 0.05 (significant). n = 30, 0.05 (significant). n = 100, far 0.05 (highly significant). moderating effect sample size. effect size produces different conclusions depending n. 2D curve show — fixed one n.
code: surface$p[surface$d == 0.5, surface$n == 10] #> [1] 0.1483047 surface$p[surface$d == 0.5, surface$n == 30] #> [1] 0.01043739 surface$p[surface$d == 0.5, surface$n == 100] #> [1] 2.481396e-06

what: Jensen’s inequality: two interpretations of the p-value
title: Comparing 2D and 3D p-Value Visualizations
text: subtle important point: p-value two different interpretations, 3D surface helps clarify. Conditional p-value (fixed d): p-value computed specific effect size. p_surface() returns: pconditional(d,n)=2[1−Ft(n−1)(dn)]p_{\text{conditional}}(d, n) = 2 \left[ 1 - F_{t(n-1)}(d \sqrt{n}) \right] d = 0.5, n = 30: Expected p-value (random d): average p-value possible observed effect sizes: 𝔼[p(dobs,n)]=∫p(dobs,n)⋅f(dobs∣d,n)ddobs\mathbb{E}[p(d_{\text{obs}}, n)] = \int p(d_{\text{obs}}, n) \cdot f(d_{\text{obs}} \mid d, n) \, dd_{\text{obs}} d = 0.5, n = 30, approximately: two values differ substantially (0.0104 vs 0.0589). due Jensen’s inequality: p-value convex function d, expected p-value larger conditional p-value. p3d package visualizes conditional p-value, consistent power analysis existing packages. expected p-value subject ongoing research.
code: p_surface(d = 0.5, n = 30)$p[1, 1] #> [1] 0.01043739 set.seed(42) n_sim <- 10000 n <- 30 d <- 0.5  p_values <- replicate(n_sim, {   x <- rnorm(n, mean = d, sd = 1)   t.test(x, mu = 0)$p.value })  mean(p_values) #> [1] 0.05887669

title: Introduction to p3d
text: p-value continuous measure statistical evidence, yet practice often reduced binary decision: p < 0.05 “significant”, p ≥ 0.05 “significant”. dichotomous thinking major contributor reproducibility crisis science. p3d package visualizes p-value single-sample t-test three-dimensional surface two parameters: Effect size (d, Cohen’s d) Sample size (n) vignette demonstrates core functionality package.

title: Introduction to p3d
text: central function package p_surface(). Given range effect sizes sample sizes, computes p-value combination: result list several components: d: vector effect sizes n: vector sample sizes p: matrix p-values (dimensions length(d) × length(n)) d_crit: critical effect sizes α = 0.05 n alpha: significance level grid: tidy data frame combinations

title: Introduction to p3d
text: example, p-value d = 0.5, n = 30 : critical effect size n = 30 : means: 30 observations, effect size least 0.37 required statistical significance α = 0.05.
code: surface$p[surface$d == 0.5, surface$n == 30] #> [1] 0.01043739 surface$d_crit[surface$n == 30] #> [1] 0.3734061

title: Introduction to p3d
text: simplest way visualize surface plot_p_static(), uses base R graphics external dependencies:  ideal PDF output, journal figures, printed reports.
code: plot_p_static(surface)

title: Introduction to p3d
text: interactive exploration, use plot_p_surface() plotly engine: Alternatively, rgl engine provides native R window: engines allow rotation, zooming, panning.
code: plot_p_surface(surface, engine = "plotly") plot_p_surface(surface, engine = "rgl")

title: Introduction to p3d
text: comparison existing 2D packages pvaluefunctions, use p_curve_2d(): 2D curve mathematically equivalent slice 3D surface fixed n.

title: Introduction to p3d
text: Let’s apply p3d real dataset. mtcars dataset contains fuel consumption (mpg) 32 automobiles. Suppose want test whether mean mpg different 20: p-value single observation : placing observation 3D surface, can see effect size behave different sample sizes:
code: x <- mtcars$mpg d_obs <- (mean(x) - 20) / sd(x) n_obs <- length(x)  cat("Observed effect size:", round(d_obs, 4), "\n") #> Observed effect size: 0.015 cat("Sample size:", n_obs, "\n") #> Sample size: 32 2 * (1 - pt(abs(d_obs) * sqrt(n_obs), df = n_obs - 1)) #> [1] 0.9327606 surface_real <- p_surface(   d = seq(-0.5, 0.5, 0.01),   n = seq(5, 200, 5) )  plot_p_static(surface_real, theta = 30, phi = 20)

title: Introduction to p3d
text: p3d package provides three-dimensional perspective p-value. visualizing p-value simultaneously across effect size sample size, reveals: continuous nature p-value (binary switch) moderating effect sample size statistical significance interaction effect size sample size complements traditional 2D visualizations helps weaken dichotomous thinking plagues statistical practice.

what: Compute p-value surface for single-sample t-test — p_surface
title: Compute p-value surface for single-sample t-test — p_surface
text: Computes p-value single-sample t-test function effect size (Cohen's d) sample size (n). Returns grid p-values suitable 3D visualization.

title: Compute p-value surface for single-sample t-test — p_surface
code: p_surface(d, n, alpha = 0.05)

title: Compute p-value surface for single-sample t-test — p_surface
text: d Numeric vector effect sizes (Cohen's d). Typical range: -2 2. n Numeric vector sample sizes. Must >= 2. Typical range: 5 200. alpha Significance level critical effect size. Default: 0.05.

title: Compute p-value surface for single-sample t-test — p_surface
text: list following elements: d input vector effect sizes. n input vector sample sizes. p matrix p-values dimensions length(d) x length(n). d_crit numeric vector critical effect sizes sample size level alpha. alpha significance level used. grid data frame full grid (d, n, p) combinations.

title: Compute p-value surface for single-sample t-test — p_surface
text: p-value computed using formula: $$p(d, n) = 2 \left[ 1 - F_{t(n-1)}(d \sqrt{n}) \right]$$ \(F_{t(n-1)}\) cumulative distribution function t-distribution \(n-1\) degrees freedom. critical effect size level \(\alpha\) : $$d_{crit}(n) = \frac{F^{-1}_{t(n-1)}(1 - \alpha/2)}{\sqrt{n}}$$
